expected.text: Hibi (日々, "day after day") tracks **claims**: sentences in documents that assert something checkable.
The documents can be anything: a README, `CLAUDE.md`, an ADR, a pricing page, a process note in a knowledge repository.
Hibi reports which claims are stale, which documents cannot be trusted right now, which sentences contradict each other, and which sentences nothing could verify.
Hibi runs no verifiers and no resolvers.
Its only network call is the judge API, and its only subprocess is `git`.
An agent collects evidence and submits it.
The primary user is a coding agent; JSON is the contract.
| kind | where its truth is observed | what makes it stale |
| `code` | one or more code spans | an anchored span changed, disappeared, or matches several places |
| `reference` | one span in another document | the span changed, or the judge finds it no longer supports the sentence |
| `attested` | outside the repository: a dashboard, a vendor page, a person | its `ttl` ran out since the last judged evidence or human vouch, or submitted evidence refutes it |
Before an agent relies on a document, it runs `hibi check --doc <file>`; exit 2 means a sentence in it is stale, and the verdicts say which one and what to do.
When it writes or reviews a document, it runs `hibi audit --doc <file>` to see which sentences are claims of which kind and records them with `hibi record`.
After a code change, `hibi check --since origin/main` names the sentences the change invalidated.
Periodically, `hibi check` lists a worklist of claims to re-check; the agent follows each claim's procedure, collects what it observed, and submits it with `hibi evidence`.
The judge decides whether the evidence supports the sentence.
Only judged evidence or a human vouch resets a claim's ttl.
## What hibi will and will not do
- **Same tree, same verdicts.** Anchor resolution is deterministic.

expected.text: Where is this document in its life?
Each has its own field and its own verbs.
Enforcement is a field on the claim.
The claim may gate (exit 2) and warn. |
Recorded with `record --suggest` (or `"suggest": true` in a `--from-file` item).
It never gates and never warns. |
Kept in the store for history.
It never gates or warns, the contradiction pass skips it, and `evidence` and `attest` refuse it. |
Sets the claim's `enforcement` to `retired` and saves it.
The claim file stays in `.claims/claims/`; do not delete it by hand.
A second call changes nothing and reports `alreadyRetired: true`.
In `check`, a retired claim is not resolved: its verdict reads `doc: "retired"` (and `evidence: "retired"` when it has an evidence side) and carries one reason, `retired claim: never gates or warns`.
It is counted in `summary.retired` and in none of `gating`, `warning`, or `clean`.
Lifecycle is a field on the document record in `.claims/documents/`.
The old document's record carries `supersededBy` with the new document's id. |
| `archived` | Moved to `archive/`, with a tombstone at the old path. |
A live claim (not retired) on a `superseded` or `archived` document is **stranded**.
A stranded claim still resolves, still gates, and still warns.
In `check` JSON, every live claim on a non-active document appears in that document's `suspect[]` with the lifecycle as its status when nothing worse applies.
Claims on a non-active document are left out of the worklist, so no agent is asked to collect evidence for them.
1. Registers `--to` in the store if needed.
`--from` must already be registered; otherwise the command fails with `document <path> is not registered`.
2. Moves every live claim on `--from` to `--to`, without reading the old file.
When a claim's stored quote occurs verbatim exactly once in `--to`, its position is updated; otherwise its anchors are left as stored.
The claim's id, sentence, quote, hashes, evidence, sources, procedure, attestations, and `ref` never change.
3. Sets `--from` to `superseded` and records `supersededBy` on it.
Each `relocated` entry is `{ claimId, doc, evidence? }` with the claim's anchor states after the move.
A sentence that was edited reads `changed`.
A sentence that is not in `--to` reads `orphaned` and gates; fix it with `hibi reanchor <id> --doc-quote "…"` or `hibi retire <id>`.
A quote found more than once is resolved by the normal resolver and may read `moved`.
`misses` lists only claims whose move failed with an error, so it is normally empty.
`strandedClaims` lists the live claims still on the old document after the pass, and is normally empty too.
A claim stays on a superseded document only when its move failed (it is listed in `misses`) or when it was recorded there after the supersede.
Copies the file to `archive/<path>`, replaces the original with a short tombstone, and sets the document's lifecycle to `archived`.
The tombstone is a Markdown page headed `# Archived` that names the old path and, with `--successor`, links to the successor.

```json
{ "ok": true, "action": "archive", "schemaVersion": "v4",
  "doc": "old.md", "archivedTo": "archive/old.md", "successor": "new.md",
  "lifecycle": "archived", "strandedClaims": ["clm_…"], "dryRun": false,
  "next": "reanchor or retire each stranded claim, then hibi check" }
```
`archivedTo` is null when the document is registered but its file was not on disk.
A path that is not a registered document (one with no record in `.claims/documents/`) is an error, and nothing is written.
To withdraw a document that has no successor, archive it without `--successor`.

```sh
hibi reanchor <claim-id> [--doc <path>] [--doc-quote <text> | --doc-range L1:L3]
                         [--code-file <path> (--code-quote <text> | --code-range L1:L9)]...
                         [--ref-file <path> (--ref-quote <text> | --ref-range L1:L3)]
                         [--suggest] [--dry-run]
hibi reanchor --moved [--doc <path>] [--dry-run]
```
`reanchor` re-resolves every span of the claim against the working tree and stores the relocated sides as the new baseline.
It refreshes the claim's `sentence` from the doc span when the doc side is relocated.
- Without span flags for a side, the side is relocated only when it reads `moved`.
A side that reads `unchanged` is kept.

- A side that reads `changed`, `ambiguous`, or `orphaned` is left as stored, and the result's `kept` gives the reason, for example `doc: changed; pass --doc-quote to re-anchor` or `evidence: orphaned; pass --code-quote to re-anchor`.
Hibi does not guess where an edited or lost span went; pass the new span.
- The command exits 0 when at least one side was relocated or no side needed relocating.
It exits 1 and writes nothing when a side needed relocating and no side was relocated.
- `--doc`, the doc span flags, and the ref span flags may each be given once.
A repeat is an error such as `--doc-quote given twice; reanchor takes one span per side`.
- A value that starts with `-` takes the `=` form: `--doc-quote="- Retries are capped at 5 attempts"`.
- `--doc <path>` with `--doc-quote` or `--doc-range` moves the claim to another document.

- `--code-file` is repeatable: each one opens a span that takes the `--code-quote` or `--code-range` after it, and the spans given replace all of a `code` claim's spans, in order; `--ref-file` with `--ref-quote` or `--ref-range` replaces a `reference` claim's span.
The wrong kind is an error, for example `claim <id> is a code claim; --ref-file, --ref-quote, and --ref-range are for reference claims.`

- An evidence side in a sibling repo that is not checked out is kept as stored, with a warning such as `evidence side api:src/limits.ts kept unchanged: sibling repo "api" is not checked out at ../api`.
- An explicit `--code-file` span in a sibling repo that is not checked out keeps the stored span for that file.
The result's `kept` lists it with `state: "unavailable"` and the reason `evidence: repository api not checked out; kept as stored`, and the command exits 0 when another side was relocated.

It applies the plain rule to every live claim in the store, or with `--doc <path>` to the live claims of that document: `moved` sides are relocated, and `changed`, `ambiguous`, and `orphaned` sides are kept and listed.
It prints one line per claim with a side relocated or kept, and exits 0.
It ranks candidate locations for the stored doc and evidence quotes.
It cannot be combined with span flags or `--dry-run`.
- `--dry-run` computes the result and writes nothing.
Reanchor only after you have re-read the sentence against its evidence.
A reanchor tells hibi that the current text is correct.
Claims belong to the document they quote.
Move them in the same change as the prose:
1. `hibi list --path <old-doc>` lists the claims that name the file on either side.
3. For each `relocated` entry that reads `changed` or `orphaned`, fix the sentence in the new document if it is wrong, then run `hibi reanchor <id> --doc-quote "…"`, or `hibi retire <id>`.
4. For each entry in `misses`, run `hibi reanchor <id> --doc <new-doc> --doc-quote "…"`, or `hibi retire <id>`.
5. When `strandedClaims` is empty, delete or archive the old file.
If you skip steps 2 to 4, the claims become `doc: orphaned` after the delete, and an orphaned enforced claim gates.
Orphaned is not retired: it is a live record that points at a missing file.
Hibi records lifecycle and enforcement and reports what is stranded or orphaned.
A person or an agent rewrites the prose, decides what to reanchor and what to retire, and runs `hibi check` again.
Two verbs write a document: `archive` copies it to `archive/` and writes the tombstone in its place, and `init --instructions` appends one line to an agent instruction file.
How enforcement and states become gates, warnings, and exit codes.

name: four-backtick fence is not closed by a three-backtick line
source: spec-derived: SPEC section 6.3 step 2, ruling 9 (fences close by CommonMark). Lines: 1 '````md', 2 '```', 3 'x. y', 4 '````', 5 '', 6 'After. More.'. Line 1: no fence open, t starts with 4 backticks, so it opens a backtick fence of length 4 (info string 'md' allowed); fence open, not a boundary. Line 2: t is 3 backticks, fewer than 4, so it does not close; fence stays open. Line 3: inside the fence. Line 4: t is 4 backticks only, at least 4, so it closes; after the update no fence is open, t is not empty, not a tag, not a thematic break: not a boundary. Line 5: empty, no fence open: boundary. Line 6: not a boundary. Blocks: lines 1-4 (fenced, it has fence lines) and line 6. Step 3/5: the fenced block is one fenced unit, range from '`' at line 1 to the end of line 4. Line 6 is one sentence piece cut after 'After.' (followed by a space): units 'After.' and 'More.'. No headings, so every headingPath is []. Under the old rule (any same-marker fence line closes) line 2 closed the fence, line 4 reopened it, and the rest of the text became one fenced unit.

name: a fence line with an info string does not close an open fence
source:
spec-derived: SPEC section 6.3 step 2, ruling 9 (a closing fence is made only of the marker character, nothing but WS after). Lines: 1 '```', 2 '```js', 3 'x', 4 '```', 5 '', 6 'After.'. Line 1 opens a backtick fence of length 3. Line 2: t '```js' holds a character other than '`', so it does not close; it is content. Line 3: content. Line 4: t is 3 backticks only, at least 3: closes; not a boundary (t not empty). Line 5: empty with no fence open: boundary. Line 6: not a boundary. Blocks: lines 1-4 (fenced) and line 6. Units: fenced '```
```js
x
```' (lines 1-4) and sentence 'After.' (line 6, no cut: '.' is not followed by WS). headingPath [] everywhere. Under the old rule line 2 closed the fence, line 4 reopened it and lines 5-6 stayed inside it: one fenced unit for the whole text.

name: BOM before --- frontmatter does not prevent recognition
source: spec-derived: SPEC section 6.3 step 1, ruling 10 (a leading U+FEFF does not prevent recognition; the BOM stays in the text). Class markdown (path a.md). Line 1 is U+FEFF then '---'; with the one leading U+FEFF set aside and trailing WS removed it is '---', so it opens frontmatter. Line 3 '---' is the next line that with trailing WS removed is '---': splitting starts after its newline, at line 4. Line 4 'Body.' is one block, one sentence piece, no cut ('.' at the end). Offsets: U+FEFF is 3 bytes and 1 UTF-16 unit, so 'Body.' is bytes 16-21 and UTF-16 14-19. Under the old rule line 1 was not '---' (U+FEFF is not WS), no frontmatter was found, and the units were the sentence U+FEFF '---\nt: 1' and 'Body.' (line 3 '---' is a thematic break).

name: +++ TOML frontmatter is skipped in .md
source:
spec-derived: SPEC section 6.3 step 1, ruling 10 (+++ frontmatter is recognised like ---). Class markdown. Line 1 with trailing WS removed is '+++': it opens frontmatter. Line 3 '+++' is the next line that with trailing WS removed is '+++': splitting starts at line 4. Line 4 'Body. More.' is one block, one sentence piece, cut after 'Body.' (followed by a space): units 'Body.' and 'More.' on line 4. Under the old rule there was no frontmatter: lines 1-4 formed one block ('+++' is no boundary and, with no WS after '+', no list marker), one sentence piece cut after 'Body.', giving '+++
t = 1
+++
Body.' and 'More.'.

name: +++ frontmatter is not closed by ---
source: spec-derived: SPEC section 6.3 steps 1 and 2, ruling 10 (+++ frontmatter is closed only by a +++ line). Class markdown. Line 1 '+++  ' with trailing WS removed is '+++': a candidate opener. The closing line must with trailing WS removed be '+++'; line 3 is '---' and there is no other line, so there is no frontmatter and splitting starts at line 1. Step 2: line 1 '+++' and line 2 't = 1' are not boundaries; line 3 '---' is a thematic break: boundary; line 4 not a boundary. Blocks: lines 1-2 and line 4. Block 1 runs from '+' at line 1 to the end of line 2 ('t = 1'); its interior trailing spaces on line 1 stay. It is one sentence piece with no terminator: one unit, lines 1-2. Block 2: 'Body.' on line 4.

name: thematic breaks with spaces or tabs between the characters separate blocks
source:
spec-derived: SPEC section 6.3 step 2, ruling 11 (a thematic break is 3 or more of one of '-', '*', '_' with only spaces or tabs between). Lines 2 '- - -', 4 '* * *' and 6 '_<TAB>_ _' are thematic breaks, so boundary lines (no fence is open). Lines 1, 3, 5, 7 are each a one-line block and one sentence piece with no cut ('.' at the end): units 'One.' (1), 'Two.' (3), 'Three.' (5), 'Four.' (7). Under the old rule (no spaces allowed) there were no boundaries: one block whose lines 2 and 4 start list-item pieces ('- ' and '* '), giving list items '- - -
Two.' and '* * *
Three.
_<TAB>_ _
Four.'.

name: mixed characters are not a thematic break
source: spec-derived: SPEC section 6.3 steps 2 to 5, ruling 11 (the break uses one character). Line 2 '- * -' mixes '-' and '*', so it is not a thematic break; no line is a boundary and lines 1-3 form one block. Step 3: line 2 with leading WS removed starts with '- ' (list marker), so it starts a piece; line 3 'More.' continues it. Pieces: line 1 (sentence, 'Text.') and lines 2-3 (list-item, from the first line '- * -'). Step 5: '- * -\nMore.' has no terminator followed by WS: one list-item unit, lines 2-3.

name: closing # run needs whitespace before it
source: spec-derived: SPEC section 6.3 step 6, ruling 12 (a closing '#' run is stripped only when preceded by WS). Line 1 '# C#' is a heading of level 1 with content 'C#'; the trailing '#' follows 'C', not WS, so it is part of the text: heading text 'C#'. Step 3: the line after a heading starts a new piece, so line 2 'Text.' is a sentence piece. Units: heading '# C#' with path [] (no ancestors), then 'Text.' with path ['C#']. Under the old rule the trailing '#' was stripped and the path was ['C'].

name: closing # run after whitespace is stripped; a heading of only a # run has empty text
source: spec-derived: SPEC section 6.3 step 6, ruling 12. Line 1 '# C #': level 1, content 'C #'; the closing '#' follows a space, so it is stripped: text 'C'. Line 2 starts a piece after the heading: sentence 'A.' with path ['C']. Line 3 '### ###' starts a piece (heading pattern): level 3, content '###', which is a '#' run only: text ''. Before it is emitted, stacked headings of level 3 or more are popped (none): path ['C']; then '' is pushed. Line 4 starts a piece after the heading: sentence 'B.' with path ['C', ''].

name: frontmatter delimiters with trailing whitespace
source: spec-derived: SPEC section 6.3 step 1. Class markdown. Line 1 '---  ' with trailing WS removed is '---': it opens frontmatter. Line 3 '--- <TAB>' with trailing WS removed is '---': it closes it; splitting starts at line 4. 'Body.' is one sentence unit on line 4.

name: two backticks are not a fence
source: spec-derived: SPEC section 6.3 steps 2 and 5. Line 1 '``' has only 2 backticks, so it is not a fence line and no fence opens. Line 3 is empty with no fence open: boundary. Blocks: lines 1-2 and line 4. Block 1 is one sentence piece '``\nA. B'. Code spans: the only backtick run '``' has no later run of 2, so it is literal and there is no span. Cut after 'A.' (followed by a space): units '``\nA.' (lines 1-2) and 'B' (line 2). Block 2: 'C.' on line 4.

name: tag line needs a letter first and whitespace before attributes
source: spec-derived: SPEC section 6.3 step 2, tag pattern ^<\/?[A-Za-z][\w.:-]*(?:\s[^<>]*)?\/?>$. Line 2 '<div class="x">': name 'div', then a space, then 'class="x"' (no '<' or '>'), then '>': a tag line, boundary. Line 4 '<div"x">': after the name 'div' comes '"', which is neither WS nor '/>' nor '>': not a tag line. Line 6 '<1a>': '1' is not a letter: not a tag line. Blocks: line 1, and lines 3-7. Step 3: no line of 4-7 starts a piece ('<' is not a piece start), so lines 3-7 are one sentence piece. Step 5: cuts after 'Two.' and 'Three.' (each followed by a newline): units 'Two.' (3), '<div"x">\nThree.' (4-5), '<1a>\nFour.' (6-7).

Two.', cut after 'One.' (followed by a newline): units 'One.' (line 1) and '--

name: > without a following space starts a piece
source: spec-derived: SPEC section 6.3 steps 3 and 4. One block (no boundary lines). Line 2 with leading WS removed matches '>\s?' (the space is optional), so it starts a new piece. Line 1 has no terminator, so without the piece cut both lines would be one unit. Pieces: 'Intro' (sentence) and '>No space.' (a blockquote line is sentence). No cuts inside either.

name: table separator whose last cell has no trailing pipe is dropped
source: spec-derived: SPEC section 6.3 step 3, separator ^\|?(?:\s*:?-+:?\s*\|)+\s*(?::?-+:?\s*)?$. One block; every line starts with '|', so each line is its own piece of kind table-row. Line 2 '|---|---': leading '|', one group '---|', then the optional last cell '---' without a trailing pipe: it matches, so the piece is dropped. Line 4 '|---|x': after the group '---|' the rest 'x' is not ':?-+:?\s*': no match, so it is a table row. No terminators: one unit per kept piece.

name: + is a list marker at a line start
source: spec-derived: SPEC section 6.3 steps 3 to 5. One block. Line 2 starts with '+ ' ([-*+]\s), so it starts a piece of kind list-item; line 1 has no terminator, so the piece cut is what separates them. Step 5: the marker is '+ ' (bytes 0-2 of the piece); the '.' after 'item' is past it and followed by a space: cut. Units: 'Intro' (sentence), '+ plus item.' and 'Two.' (list-item).

name: list marker needs whitespace after it
source: spec-derived: SPEC section 6.3 steps 3 and 4. One block. Lines 2 '-x one', 3 '+y two' and 4 '1.z three.' do not match [-*+]\s or \d+[.)]\s (no WS after the marker), nor any other piece start: one sentence piece. The '.' in '1.z' is followed by 'z' and the final '.' by nothing: no cut. One unit, lines 1-4.
